strengths: Emotion-conditioned image editing is a worthwhile computer-vision problem. The simple source-image-plus-emotion interface is useful, and qualitative examples demonstrate changes beyond global color transfer.

EmoPair provides 338,544 paired examples and could become a useful research resource. The manuscript credits InstructPix2Pix and EmoSet and describes instruction selection and filtering for the generated subset.

The human evaluation provides evidence beyond classifier scores: Figure 5 reports 56% aggregate online preference for EmoEditor. Randomized comparisons, attention checks, and a supplementary laboratory study strengthen the empirical effort.
The extensive visualizations help explain the approach. The discussion appropriately acknowledges semantic drift, facial-detail failures, and potential misuse for emotional manipulation.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative evaluation is strongly coupled to the method. The same predictor P labels or filters training data, selects outputs during up to 30 inference iterations, and supplies EMR, ESR, and ENRD. Table 1 shows EMR increasing from 5.06% without P to 50.20% with the full method, making independent validation especially important. Human ablations and an independently trained evaluator are needed to distinguish improved emotional editing from improved agreement with P.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. InstructPix2Pix receives single-word prompts, while EmoEditor receives task-specific training and repeated inference. Comparisons with the same-data emotion-conditioned InstructPix2Pix baseline, and LMS using an equivalent critic/search budget, would clarify the architectural benefit. The closely related Affective Image Filter is cited but not evaluated; inference time and typical iteration counts are also missing.

The training objective is underspecified in a consequential place. Section 3.2 defines z as the source-image latent and noises that latent, but never explains how the paired target image enters the diffusion loss. Taken literally, this trains source reconstruction. The source and target latent roles need clarification. Section S2.2 also omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, and sampling settings, limiting reproducibility.

ESR is not mathematically valid as written under the conventional KL-divergence argument order: KL(e_g, e_oh) is infinite when the predicted distribution assigns positive probability to categories where the one-hot target is zero. The authors should specify the actual divergence direction or smoothing and verify the reported results. This may be a correctable definition error, but ESR currently cannot be reproduced.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed the demonstrated novelty. The described image conditioning and cross-attention closely resemble the underlying InstructPix2Pix machinery. Moreover, the emotion encoder depends only on the emotion label, so its alignment loss learns a shared instruction prior for each category; this does not establish the claimed image-specific human-like or neuro-symbolic reasoning. Relevant architectural controls are absent.

The joint goal of changing emotion while preserving scene semantics is insufficiently validated. Human participants judge emotional effect without assessing preservation against the source; classifier-derived saliency and edge differences do not establish semantic consistency. Most dataset labels are automatic, without a reported human audit, and Figure S3 includes substantial content replacements, such as food becoming a landscape. Quantitative evaluation also concentrates on cross-valence EmoSet transfers; within-valence and neutral-image generalization remain illustrative.

The human results warrant narrower claims and clearer reporting. Against LMS, preference is 54% online, 49% in the laboratory, and 50% for online transfers to positive emotions (Figure S7). The supplement reports that only 27% of online participants passed screening, so final participant/trial counts and the treatment of repeated participant/image judgments in uncertainty estimates should be explicit. The stated 417,000 trials should also be corrected to 41,700 before filtering; that arithmetic correction alone would not affect the recommendation.
